I could describe what I wanted and get a working first version to react to, which is a much better place to think from than an empty editor.

It is at its best on the well-trodden stuff: wiring, plumbing, the parts of an app that thousands of people have written before. When I needed a standard piece of Mac app scaffolding or a fiddly bit of glue code, the assistant produced it quickly and I moved on. That is real time saved, and more importantly, it kept me in the interesting decisions rather than lost in mechanics.

Trying things also got cheaper. When you can spin up a rough version of an idea in minutes, you try three approaches instead of committing to the first one because it was expensive to build. That changed how I explored the design, not just how fast I typed.

Where I had to slow it down

The flip side is that a confident assistant will happily take a big leap in the wrong direction. Left unchecked, it generates a lot of plausible code at once, and if the direction is off, you now have a large, plausible-looking mistake to unpick. That is worse than a small one, because it looks fine until you look closely.

What worked for me was insisting on small, verifiable steps. Build one thing, run it, confirm it does what I meant, then move on. The discipline is the same one I use for writing documents: let the AI do the heavy lifting, but keep the steps small enough that you can actually check them. When I let it run too far ahead, I paid for it later.

Correctness is still on me. The assistant does not know whether the app is right, only whether the code plausibly does what I asked. Knowing whether what I asked for was the right thing, and whether the result actually behaves, is judgement, and judgement did not get automated.

What actually changed about the work

The bottleneck moved. It used to sit in the typing: knowing the exact syntax, remembering the API, getting the code out of your head and onto the screen. Now that part is cheap, and the bottleneck sits in knowing what you want. Deciding what to build, what to leave out, what "good" looks like for this particular app. Those decisions became the whole job, which is as it should be.

There is a nice symmetry here with the app itself. htmlEdit exists because AI is great at producing a document but the last mile of finishing it is judgement, better done by hand than by re-prompting. Building the app taught me the same lesson from the other side: AI is great at producing code, but the last mile of deciding whether it is right is still yours. In both cases the tool gets you most of the way, fast, and the value you add is at the edges.

Would I do it again

Without hesitation. The app is open source and you can read every line of it, warts and all, on the site. It is a genuinely different way to build: less time spent on mechanics, more spent on decisions. But it is not magic, and treating it as magic is how people end up with confident nonsense. Keep the steps small, own the judgement, and let it take the drudgery. That balance is the whole skill.

If you are using AI to make documents rather than software, the same instinct applies. I wrote about the draft-to-done workflow for exactly that.

title: Small Tools, Big Leverage: The Case for Single-Purpose Apps
metaDescription: Sprawling all-in-one platforms promise everything and master nothing. Here is the case for small, single-purpose tools that do one job properly.
tldr: A tool that does one thing well beats a bloated platform that does ten things adequately. Small single-purpose apps are easier to learn, faster to use, and harder to get wrong.
keyTakeaways: Single-purpose tools have a shallower learning curve and less to go wrong.
All-in-one platforms optimise for feature checklists, not for your task.
Small tools compose: you can chain them however you like.
You keep control and ownership instead of renting a walled garden.
The best tool often just does the one annoying step nobody else covers.
bodyHtml:
If you have a specific, annoying job to do, a small tool built for exactly that job will almost always beat a sprawling platform that lists it as feature number thirty-seven. The single-purpose app has one thing to get right, so it usually gets it right. The all-in-one suite has a thousand things to get roughly right, and roughly right is where most of them live.

We have been trained to want the opposite. Bigger feels safer. One login, one subscription, one vendor, one place for everything. But the everything-app promise has a catch that shows up the moment you actually try to do the one thing you came for.

Why big tools feel heavy

A platform that does ten jobs has to make ten compromises. Every screen has to accommodate ten workflows, so every button is a little further from where you need it. The onboarding has to teach ten things, so it teaches all of them shallowly. The settings menu is enormous because it has to be. You spend your first hour learning the tool instead of doing the work.

There is a behavioural point buried in here. Big tools are often designed to win a feature comparison, not to make your task fast. A checklist of two hundred features sells the deal. But you do not use two hundred features. You use three, badly served, surrounded by the other one hundred and ninety-seven you are paying for and stepping around.

A small tool has none of that weight. It opens, it does the thing, you leave. The learning curve is a step, not a hill. There is less to break, less to update, less to hold in your head.

Small tools compose

The real magic of single-purpose tools is that they combine. This is the old idea behind the command line: lots of little programs that each do one thing, piped together however the moment requires. You are not locked into one vendor's idea of your workflow. You assemble your own.

The AI era makes this more relevant, not less. A model might draft your document, another tool might turn it into HTML, and then you need one specific thing: to fix the rendered result without wrestling raw code. That is a job for a tool that does only that. htmlEdit is deliberately narrow: it lets you edit an AI-generated HTML document visually, by clicking and typing on the page, and nothing else. It does not want to be your email client, your CRM, or your operating system. It does the one step the big tools skip.

That narrowness is the feature. Because it only does one thing, it can slot into whatever chain you have without asking you to move your whole life into it.

Ownership beats renting

Small, focused tools also tend to respect you more. There is less incentive to trap you, because the pitch is competence, not lock-in. Many are open source, run locally, and keep your data on your machine. You are using a tool, not moving into a walled garden and paying rent on your own work.

Compare that to the platform that owns your files, your history and your habits, and quietly raises the price once you cannot leave. The switching cost is the business model. With a small tool, if something better comes along, you just use the better thing. Nothing is holding you hostage.

None of this means every job wants a boutique tool. Some things genuinely benefit from integration, and there is a real cost to juggling twenty logins. But the default assumption, that bigger and more unified is automatically better, deserves more suspicion than it gets. For most specific, recurring annoyances, the right answer is a small sharp tool that does that one thing and gets out of your way.

The next time you reach for the giant platform to solve a narrow problem, ask what you actually need. Often it is one clean step. And the tool that does only that step will beat the one that does everything.

title: The Future of Documents: Editable, Portable, AI-Native
metaDescription: Documents are being remade by AI. The winning format will be editable by hand, portable across tools, and native to the web. Here is what that looks like.
tldr: The document of the future is AI-native but human-editable, portable rather than trapped in a vendor's format, and built on the open web. HTML is quietly becoming that format.
keyTakeaways: AI generates documents fast, so editing and control become the bottleneck.
Proprietary formats trap your work; open formats travel freely.
HTML is already universal, styleable, and AI-native.
The winning document is one you can hand-edit without touching code.
Portability and privacy will matter more as AI output volume rises.
bodyHtml:
The document is being quietly rebuilt, and the version that wins will have three properties: it will be easy to edit by hand, it will travel freely between tools, and it will be native to the web rather than locked in one company's file format. AI is the force driving this, but the shape of the outcome is not really about AI. It is about who controls the output once the AI has done its bit.

For thirty years the document meant a proprietary file you opened in the program that made it. The format was the moat. Your work lived inside a vendor's box, and moving it out meant conversions, broken formatting and lost fidelity. That model is now under real pressure, because the way documents come into existence has changed.

AI makes generation cheap, so control gets scarce

When producing a first draft took an hour, the value was in the writing. Now a decent draft appears in seconds. That does not make documents less important. It moves the scarce, valuable work downstream, to editing, judgement and control. When anyone can generate ten versions of anything, the person who can quickly shape the right one has the advantage.

This is why the future document has to be genuinely editable by a human, not just re-promptable. Re-prompting is coarse. It swaps the whole thing when you wanted to change a line. A document you can put your hands into, adjust precisely and leave otherwise untouched, is a document you actually control. As I have argued in the case for editing over regenerating, that last mile of handwork is where the value now sits.

Portable beats proprietary

The second property is portability. AI does not respect your vendor boundaries. It will happily generate a document, then hand it to another tool to restyle, then another to publish. That pipeline only works if the document is in a format everything can read and write. A proprietary format is friction at every handoff. An open one is a clean pipe.

This is a straightforward prediction: the documents that thrive will be the ones that move without permission. No export step, no fidelity loss, no "please upgrade to open this file." Just a format that every tool, every browser and every model already understands.

Why HTML is quietly winning

Here is the slightly unfashionable claim: that format is HTML. It is not new or exciting, and that is exactly why it works. HTML is already the most universal document format on earth. Every device renders it. It styles beautifully. It carries structure, links and layout. And AI models are extremely comfortable producing it, because the web is what they learned from. When you ask a model for a nicely formatted document, HTML is often what it reaches for naturally.

HTML is, in other words, already AI-native and already portable. It ticks two of the three boxes without anyone planning it. The missing box has always been the editing experience. Raw HTML is hostile to normal humans. If changing a heading means finding the right tag in a wall of markup, the format fails the hand-editable test, and people fall back to re-prompting or copying into a word processor and losing the formatting.

Close that gap and HTML becomes the complete package. This is the specific problem htmlEdit exists to solve: it lets you edit a rendered HTML document by pointing, clicking and typing, the way you would in a word processor, so you get the portability and AI-friendliness of HTML without ever touching the code. The document stays open, editable and yours.

What this adds up to

Put the pieces together and the future document looks like this. It is generated with AI assistance, so it starts fast. It is HTML, so it is portable and universal. It is editable by hand without code, so you keep control of the final result. And increasingly it is handled locally and privately, because as the volume of AI output rises, so does the value of not shipping every draft to someone else's server.

None of this requires a grand new standard. The pieces already exist. What is changing is which properties matter. For years we optimised documents for the program that made them. We are about to optimise them for movement, editability and the open web instead. That is a better set of priorities, and it puts you, not the vendor, back in charge of your own work.
